title: Our CMA forecasts, amid a flurry of punches - Barclays Private Bank
text: Barclays Home Contact us Log in Menu Our CMA forecasts, amid a flurry of punches MULTI-ASSET PORTFOLIO ALLOCATION Nikola Vasiljevic, Ph.D., Head of Global Asset Allocation, Zurich, Switzerland; Lukas Gehrig, Head of Quant Macro and Thematic Strategy, Zurich, Switzerland Share page via Facebook Share page via X Share page via LinkedIn Share page via email Please note: This article is more technical in nature than our typical articles, and may require some background knowledge and experience in investing to understand the themes that we explore below. All data referenced in this article is sourced from Bloomberg unless otherwise stated, and is accurate at the time of publishing. Key points Our updated capital market assumptions suggest that this year’s market upheavals will have limited effects on asset returns over the next decade Despite the heightened uncertainty and rich current valuations, equities will remain the main driver of long-term multi-asset portfolio returns In the bond world, returns are largely driven by yield expectations. However, with credit spreads tight, high yield bonds may struggle to match their historical performance Commodities, hedge funds, private credit and other illiquid alternative assets will continue to provide ways to diversify portfolios and help long-term investors to stay aloof of the short-term noise. How can one decide how to invest over a 10-year horizon, when even the next week is ripe with uncertainty? Perhaps two contrasting words of wisdom from two different heavyweights might help to address this very topical issue – formulated by Mike Tyson and Warren Buffett. Mike Tyson famously said that “everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth” in an interview before a fight with rival Evander Holyfield. Warren Buffett, a treasure trove of investing titbits, is quoted as saying that “the stock market is a device for transferring money from the impatient to the patient”. Unlike a boxing match, in investing, short-term uncertainty does not necessarily translate into the long term, given that fundamentals evolve slowly and tend to pull volatile prices back from extremes. Reassessing the fundamentals The views we base our forecasts on, however, have to be updated with some regularity. Starting from the ingredients of economic growth, workers, capital and productivity to the stance of fiscal and monetary policy, the structure of bond markets, and growth and valuation perspectives for equities and other asset classes. Our key takeaways from this year’s review of our long-term assumptions are as follows: The world’s leading economies are on divergent tracks Government bonds offer enough return to crowd out many, but not all, liquid alternatives Equities remain at the core for long-term returns Illiquid alternatives, hedge funds in particular, tend to thrive in this setting. Different stages in the economic cycle Not only are the short-term woes of the world’s leading economies different, as examined in Shaken but not stirred, the long-term prospects for these economies differ as well. The US economy is given a long-term growth potential above 2.5% – below the post-pandemic growth surge but significantly above the European long-term potential of closer to 1.5%. The difference between the two blocs boils down to demographics and productivity increases. All key eurozone economies are facing an expected decrease in their working age population, which is unlikely to be offset by increases in labour force participation. And the quicker adoption of new technologies (and more liberal labour laws) are expected to favour the US in the productivity race. Chinese long-term growth prospects continue to wither and are now pencilled in at around 3.5%, while India is still expected to grow at above 6% per annum over the coming decade. In terms of monetary policy, which dictates the returns of cash and short-term bonds, the starting points differ, with the European Central Bank having almost completed their current cutting cycle while the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England are on track to cut rates towards our neutral rate estimates (1) of just below 3% and around 3%, respectively (2) . Combining very uncertain near-term projections with structurally-driven long-term ones, suggests that a conversion of growth paths in the developed world is unlikely (see table), and discrepancies in both real growth and real short-term cash rates are likely to be defining features in the coming decade. While they can be battered temporarily, as long as defaults are avoided, fixed income instruments reward the patient. Current levels are high in historical comparisons, which is reflected in the differences between expected returns for government debt and investment grade peers and their respective long-term averages (see chart). Credit spreads, however, are tight historically, which adds potential risk of spread widening to the riskier segments of the fixed income universe. As such, high yield credit in particular is expected to perform below the historical average seen since 2005. Our expectations for government and investment grade bonds over the next decade lie at around 3.0% for the eurozone and between 4.5 and 5.2% for US and UK bonds. Expectations for high yield debt returns lie only 1%-1.5% higher. Equities: short-term risk, long-term growth Equities rely to a large extent on growing company earnings to drive returns, whether those are realised within the investment horizon or beyond that, and subsequently priced into them. Over the last five years, anticipated earnings growth has pushed valuations much higher, especially in US markets. This year’s tariff turmoil has led to some backpedalling on future growth prospects, as the twists and turns of US trade policy initially sparked a sell-off in markets, before an equally violent rebound in valuations. Despite that, valuations look slightly healthier than last year, weighing less on a long-term outlook. Still, economic improvements need to be recorded in order for equities not to appear expensive anymore. Real growth prospects are muted over our forecast period, especially in Europe (see chart). On balance, expected returns in developed markets are at long-term averages or below, with figures between 6% and 8%, depending on the region. Thus, for those that can look beyond near-term volatility, equities should remain the core drivers of returns. Long-term return projections: 2025-2034 Ten-year return expectations (markers) and 20-year historical arithmetic average returns (bars) for core asset classes. Historical averages from February 2005 to January 2025. Estimates for 2025-2034 Source: Barclays Private Bank and Wealth Management, May 2025. Forecasts are not a reliable indicator of future performance. CMA expected returns and volatilities are annualised and given in local currencies (or in USD in the case of asset classes that have exposure to different countries and/or regions). The value of investments can fall as well as rise and you may get back less than you invested. Liquid alternatives: buoyed by cash, trumped by bonds Expected returns for commodities of 1.7% are significantly ahead of the historical averages of the last 20 years. Over the last five years, however, returns of a broad commodity basket have exceeded 11% per annum. These contrasting observations highlight why the asset class should generally form a (small) part of a portfolio: its purpose is to provide diversification benefits, especially during inflationary shocks. Buoyed by relatively high returns on cash and solid equity returns, alternative trading strategies are expected to return 3.9% over the next 10 years, which is significantly higher than the long-term average. But returns of the asset class itself may matter less than the comparison to government bonds, which should provide higher expected returns and lower correlation to equities and high yield bonds. Illiquid alternatives: cost and benefit of illiquidity Hedge funds and private markets, including private equity, debt, real estate and infrastructure, are expected to do relatively well over the next decade. The former, especially those that act as substitutes to equities and credit in a portfolio, tends to thrive in high-rate environments. Across all hedge fund roles, we expect returns of around 6.5% on average. Risk mitigators and diversifiers among such assets are likely to digest market volatility better than liquid alternatives – also due to the fact that by construction, they are vehicles for the patient. Private market returns largely follow the performance of their public market peers with an illiquidity premium added on top. We estimate that this premium lies between 0.5% and 3.0%, with direct real estate at the low end and buyout funds – the most prevalent private equity strategy – at the high end. With fund terms between seven and 12 years, these investments are meant for experienced, patient investors and in the illiquidity premium, such long-term horizons even have a price. Illiquidity premia converged after the GFC Quarterly 10-year rolling illiquidity premia from 2010 to 2024 computed as the difference in geometric returns between illiquid benchmarks and public equivalent (US high yield bonds, US equities and global REITs) Source: Barclays Private Bank and Wealth Management, May 2025 Stick to the plan, especially when punched in the mouth While being knocked down is never a pleasant experience, one should keep in mind that investing is not a boxing match where fatigue accumulates over time. The barrage of news flow may seem overwhelming at times, but by recalibrating our long-term views, this can help to provide a solid footing for investors’ plans. Mid-Year Outlook 2025 After US tariffs sparked violent swings in financial markets, our bumper Mid-Year Outlook 2025 examines what might drive sentiment in coming months. Mid-Year Outlook 2025 Important information Neutral rates, sometimes referred to as r*, estimate the rate a central bank would set if an economy was in balance with inflation neither accelerating nor decelerating.
